USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue negotiating within the 90-day G20 truce window to the March 1 deadline, holding our existing ~$250B tariff package as leverage while pushing China to convert goodwill gestures (agricultural purchases, Qualcomm/NXP, fentanyl and IP reform rhetoric) into concrete, verifiable commitments. Do not escalate to the threatened 25% hike on the $200B list now — that would rupture talks and re-ignite the market and confidence shock — but equally do not roll back tariffs before China delivers structural concessions. Maintain the current posture, extract deliverables, and keep the deal timeline alive.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but not existential. The tariff escalation is already biting US sentiment and markets: Treasury 10-year yields fell from ~3.2% in October to 2.74%, VIX spiked to the low 30s in December, and University of Michigan consumer sentiment dropped to 91.2 from 98.3 (country_health). The web evidence confirms 2018 delivered the worst December for stocks since 1931, the S&P briefly dipped into bear-market territory on an intraday basis, and tariff uncertainty is 'chilling US business confidence' — a direct political liability since this administration is judged on market and GDP performance. That justifies a positive but modest threat reading (~+0.25): material market fragility and domestic pressure, but no supply-chain crisis, no material GDP contraction yet, and no loss of US leverage. The action stance is negotiate/hold (0.0) because the US retains clear leverage — tariffs on ~$250B remain in place, the G20 truce (2018-12-01) and resumption of Beijing talks (2019-01-07) show Beijing is engaging and making concessions — while escalating further would be self-destructive given the fragile market and could squander an opening where China is already offering purchases and tonal reform. The Meng Wanzhou arrest and Canada's retaliatory detention of the two Canadians add a tech-war/hostage dimension that argues for managing the file carefully rather than inflaming it. A full rollback or new purchase-only capitulation is premature because structural IP/tech-transfer issues—the core US demand—remain unresolved.
key_factors: 90-day G20 truce active, March 1 deadline; ~$250B US tariffs and ~$110B Chinese retaliation still in place
January 2019 market fragility: S&P worst December since 1931, VIX ~30, 10Y yield down to 2.74% from ~3.2%
Consumer sentiment fell to 91.2 from 98.3; industrial production edged lower; Baa spreads widened
China made goodwill gestures (ag purchases, Qualcomm/NXP, fentanyl, IP rhetoric) but structural reforms unresolved
Huawei CFO Meng arrest and Canadian detention (Kovrig/Spavor) add tech-war/hostage friction
Escalating to 25% now risks collapsing talks and re-triggering the market shock; full concession premature

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires: Trump-Xi agree to 90-day negotiation window; Jan 1 tariff hike to 25% suspended. Same day Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou; China demands release.
Trade talks resume in Beijing; China discusses increased purchases of US goods; structural issues remain open.
US consumer sentiment fell to 91.2 in Jan 2019 from 98.3 in Dec 2018.
US 10Y yield declined from ~3.2% (early Oct 2018) to 2.74% (early Jan 2019).
Worst December since 1931; S&P briefly in bear market territory; VIX closed 30.11; tariff/trade-war uncertainty dented investor confidence.
Threat of escalating trade war has chilled US business confidence; managers uncertain how to restructure global supply chains.
Progress on trade front but deterioration in tech war; Meng arrest; March 1 hard deadline endorsed by Trump; structural IP changes remain the sticking point.
